title: Elbow osteoarthritis and frailty: kitchen tasks with less pain (UK)

content:
Elbow osteoarthritis is less common than hip, knee or hand osteoarthritis, but it can make everyday kitchen tasks such as lifting a kettle, carrying a pan or reaching into a cupboard painful. Combined with frailty, these tasks can feel tiring and less safe.

This guide explains common problems and practical ways to make kitchen tasks easier. It is educational information, not a diagnosis.

How elbow osteoarthritis affects you

Common symptoms include pain, stiffness, reduced ability to fully straighten or bend the elbow, and sometimes a catching or locking feeling. Lifting with the arm out straight and twisting movements, such as turning a tap or a jar lid, can be especially painful.

Protecting your elbows

  • Carry things close to your body, with your elbow bent, rather than at arm's length.
  • Use two hands where possible.
  • Slide pans and dishes along the worktop instead of lifting.
  • Keep the items you use most between waist and shoulder height.
  • Use lighter pans, mugs and plates.

Useful equipment

  • A kettle tipper or a one-cup hot water dispenser.
  • A trolley to move food and drinks between rooms.
  • Jar and bottle openers, and tap turners.
  • Lightweight saucepans with two handles, and a chip basket or slotted spoon to drain vegetables instead of lifting a full pan.
  • A perching stool so you can sit while preparing food.

Pacing kitchen tasks

Spread cooking across the day, sit down for preparation, and batch-cook on better days. Ready-prepared vegetables, frozen meals and meal delivery services can help on difficult days.

Treatment and exercise

NICE recommends exercise and advice as core treatments for osteoarthritis. A physiotherapist can show you gentle movements to keep the elbow moving. Topical anti-inflammatory gels may help some people. Ask a pharmacist or GP what is suitable, especially if you take other medicines.

Getting help

An occupational therapist can assess your kitchen and suggest equipment or adaptations. Ask your GP for a referral, or contact your council for a care needs assessment.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Should I wear an elbow support?

Some people find a support helpful for comfort. Ask a physiotherapist before using one regularly.

Is it safe to keep using my arm?

Usually yes. Keeping it moving helps, but avoid heavy lifting and movements that cause sharp pain.

Could it be something else?

A hot, swollen elbow, or a sudden loss of movement, needs prompt assessment.
